title: What is two-phase commit (2PC/XA) — the prepare (voting) phase then the commit phase coordinated by a transaction coordinator — why is it a blocking protocol (if the coordinator crashes after everyone votes YES, participants hold locks indefinitely), and why do most microservice architectures prefer a Saga + eventual consistency over 2PC?
shortTitle: What is two-phase commit (2PC/XA) and why Sagas are preferred

s1_definition.profdef: Two-phase commit (2PC), usually implemented over the XA standard, is an atomic-commit protocol in which a transaction coordinator drives all participants through two phases: a prepare (voting) phase where each participant durably prepares its changes and votes yes or no, and a commit phase where, if all voted yes, the coordinator tells everyone to commit, otherwise to abort. It guarantees atomicity across multiple resources but is a blocking, synchronous protocol — participants hold their locks from the moment they vote yes until they receive the final decision, so if the coordinator crashes after a unanimous yes, participants remain blocked holding locks indefinitely. Because of this blocking behavior, poor scalability, and tight availability coupling, most microservice architectures prefer a Saga with eventual consistency.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India trying to move money across two separate banks in one perfectly atomic step. A referee (the coordinator) asks both banks, "Are you ready to commit this transfer? Lock the money and tell me yes or no." Both lock the funds and say yes. Now both are frozen, holding the money locked, waiting for the referee to shout "commit." If the referee has a heart attack right then, both banks sit there with the money locked, unable to release or complete it, possibly for hours, because they dare not decide alone. That frozen waiting is the blocking problem. A Saga avoids the referee entirely: each bank does its own step and, if something later fails, posts a correcting entry to undo it — nobody ever holds everyone else's locks.
s1_definition.oneliner: 2PC trades availability for perfect atomicity by making everyone hold locks until a single coordinator decides, and if that coordinator dies mid-decision they stay locked — which is why microservices prefer Sagas and eventual consistency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two-phase commit (2PC), usually implemented over the XA standard, is an atomic-commit protocol in which a transaction coordinator drives all participants through two phases: a prepare (voting) phase where each participant durably prepares its changes and votes yes or no, and a commit phase where, if all voted yes, the coordinator tells everyone to commit, otherwise to abort. It guarantees atomicity across multiple resources but is a blocking, synchronous protocol — participants hold their locks from the moment they vote yes until they receive the final decision, so if the coordinator crashes after a unanimous yes, participants remain blocked holding locks indefinitely. Because of this blocking behavior, poor scalability, and tight availability coupling, most microservice architectures prefer a Saga with eventual consistency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India trying to move money across two separate banks in one perfectly atomic step. A referee (the coordinator) asks both banks, "Are you ready to commit this transfer? Lock the money and tell me yes or no." Both lock the funds and say yes. Now both are frozen, holding the money locked, waiting for the referee to shout "commit." If the referee has a heart attack right then, both banks sit there with the money locked, unable to release or complete it, possibly for hours, because they dare not decide alone. That frozen waiting is the blocking problem. A Saga avoids the referee entirely: each bank does its own step and, if something later fails, posts a correcting entry to undo it — nobody ever holds everyone else's locks.

**One line to remember:** 2PC trades availability for perfect atomicity by making everyone hold locks until a single coordinator decides, and if that coordinator dies mid-decision they stay locked — which is why microservices prefer Sagas and eventual consistency.

sections.s2_technical:
The protocol has two phases driven by a transaction coordinator. In phase one, the prepare or voting phase, the coordinator sends a prepare message to every participant. Each participant does all the work needed to guarantee it can commit — writes changes to a durable log, acquires and holds the necessary locks — and then votes yes (prepared) or no (cannot commit). Crucially, after voting yes, a participant has promised it will commit if told to, so it must keep its locks held and cannot unilaterally change its mind. In phase two, the commit or decision phase, if every participant voted yes the coordinator writes a commit decision and tells all participants to commit; if any voted no (or timed out), it tells them all to abort. Once a participant gets the decision, it commits or rolls back and releases its locks.

The protocol is correct in the sense that it guarantees atomicity: either all participants commit or all abort. XA is the standard interface (based on the X/Open DTP model) that lets heterogeneous resource managers — databases, JMS brokers — participate under one coordinator, and in the Java world JTA with an XA transaction manager like Atomikos or Narayana implements it.

The problem is that 2PC is a blocking protocol with a specific, dangerous failure mode. Between voting yes and receiving the decision, every participant is in an uncertain, prepared state, holding locks and unable to proceed. If the coordinator crashes after collecting a unanimous yes but before broadcasting the decision, the participants have no way to safely decide on their own — committing could violate atomicity if the coordinator actually decided to abort, and aborting could violate it if the coordinator decided to commit — so they must wait for the coordinator to recover, holding locks the entire time. In a high-throughput banking system, rows and connections locked for an indefinite period cause cascading timeouts and effectively take the system down. Heuristic decisions (a participant unilaterally guessing) exist but can break atomicity and require manual reconciliation.

Beyond the headline failure mode, 2PC has structural downsides for microservices. It is synchronous and chatty, with multiple network round trips, so latency is high and throughput is low. Availability is coupled to the weakest link: if any single participant or the coordinator is down or slow, the whole transaction stalls, which is the opposite of the fault isolation microservices are meant to provide. It also assumes participants expose a transactional, XA-capable interface, which many modern resources — REST services, most NoSQL stores, Kafka in typical use — simply do not.

For these reasons the microservices default is a Saga plus eventual consistency. Instead of one global, locked, all-or-nothing transaction, a Saga is a sequence of independent local transactions, each committed immediately in its own service and database, with no global lock. If a later step fails, the Saga runs compensating transactions that semantically undo the earlier committed steps. This keeps each service independently available and scalable, avoids any participant holding another's locks, and works with non-XA resources, at the price of eventual consistency and the design effort of writing compensations. A senior engineer keeps 2PC in their back pocket for the narrow case of a few truly XA-capable resources under one operator where atomicity is non-negotiable and the scale is modest, but reaches for Sagas for cross-service business operations, which is almost always.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India must move Rs.50000 from Rajesh's account (SAV2001) to Priya's account (CUR3001), where the two accounts live in two separate databases owned by two services. The question is how to make this atomic.

Problem 1 — The naive 2PC approach asks both account databases to prepare and lock the rows, then commit. If the coordinator crashes after both vote yes, both rows stay locked indefinitely and no other transfer touching those accounts can proceed. This is exactly the blocking, locks-held-indefinitely failure mode of two-phase commit, and we will demonstrate it by simulating a coordinator crash between prepare and commit.

Problem 2 — The Saga alternative commits each step locally with no global lock. The debit commits immediately in Rajesh's service; the credit commits immediately in Priya's service; if the credit fails, a compensating credit returns Rajesh's money. No row is ever held locked waiting on a remote coordinator, so the system stays available.

Problem 3 — The trade-off is that for a brief moment after the debit and before the credit, the total money across the two services is temporarily "in flight," which is eventual consistency. We accept this because the alternative — freezing accounts whenever a coordinator hiccups — is far worse operationally.

What the code will do: a runnable demo implements a tiny `TwoPhaseCommitCoordinator` with `prepare()` and `commit()` over two `XaParticipant` resources, and shows both the happy path and a simulated coordinator crash after the unanimous yes, leaving participants stuck in PREPARED with locks held. Then a `SagaTransfer` implements the same transfer as two local commits with a compensating action on failure, showing no locks are held across services.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Rs.50000 transfer from Rajesh (SAV2001, Rs.1,000,000) to Priya (CUR3001, Rs.250,000), run under 2PC twice and then as a Saga.

Step 1 (2PC happy path): The coordinator sends prepare to both participants. Rajesh's participant stages a debit, locks his row, and votes yes; Priya's participant stages a credit, locks her row, and votes yes. Both rows are now LOCKED, waiting.

Step 2 (2PC happy path): All voted yes, so the coordinator broadcasts commit. Both participants apply their staged change and release their locks. Rajesh is Rs.950,000, Priya is Rs.300,000, both FREE. Atomic and correct.

Step 3 (2PC crash): The coordinator again collects two yes votes, so both rows are LOCKED. Then the coordinator crashes before broadcasting the decision. Neither participant can safely decide alone, so both stay in the LOCKED, prepared state. The log shows both STUCK with locks held indefinitely — any other transfer touching these accounts is now blocked. This is the blocking failure mode.

Step 4 (Saga success): The debit is committed locally in Rajesh's service immediately, and his lock is released at once — Rs.950,000. Then the credit is committed locally in Priya's service — Rs.300,000. No global lock was ever held across services.

Step 5 (Saga failure): The debit commits locally (Rajesh to Rs.920,000 for a Rs.30000 transfer), then the credit step fails. The Saga runs a compensating credit, returning Rajesh's Rs.30,000, restoring him to Rs.950,000. No coordinator, no held locks, and the money is consistent again.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two-phase commit is an atomic-commit protocol run by a transaction coordinator over two phases. In the prepare or voting phase, the coordinator asks every participant to durably stage its changes, hold its locks, and vote yes or no. In the commit phase, if every participant voted yes the coordinator tells them all to commit, and otherwise to abort. XA is the standard interface that lets heterogeneous resources like databases and message brokers take part, and in Java it is implemented through JTA with a transaction manager such as Narayana or Atomikos. It genuinely guarantees atomicity across those resources — either everyone commits or everyone aborts.

The reason it is dangerous is that it is a blocking protocol with one very specific failure mode. After a participant votes yes, it has promised to commit if told to, so it must keep its locks held and cannot decide on its own. If the coordinator crashes after collecting a unanimous yes but before it broadcasts the decision, the participants are stranded in the prepared state: committing might violate atomicity if the coordinator had actually decided to abort, and aborting might violate it the other way, so they have no safe unilateral choice and must simply wait, holding their locks, possibly for a very long time. In a high-throughput bank, rows and connections locked indefinitely cause cascading timeouts and can take the whole system down. On top of that, 2PC is synchronous and chatty with high latency, its availability is coupled to the slowest or weakest participant, and it assumes every participant exposes an XA-capable transactional interface, which REST services, most NoSQL stores, and Kafka in normal use simply do not.

That is why most microservice architectures prefer a Saga with eventual consistency. Instead of one global, locked, all-or-nothing transaction, a Saga is a sequence of independent local transactions, each committed immediately in its own service and database with no global lock, and if a later step fails I run compensating transactions that semantically undo the earlier committed steps. No participant ever holds another's locks, so each service stays independently available and scalable, and it works with non-XA resources. The cost is eventual consistency and the effort of designing compensations.

I demonstrated this concretely for transfers at National Bank of India. Under 2PC, when I simulated the coordinator crashing right after both account participants voted yes, both account rows stayed locked indefinitely and every other transfer touching those accounts was blocked. Under the Saga version, the debit committed locally in Rajesh's service and released its lock immediately, the credit committed locally in Priya's service, and when I forced the credit to fail, a compensating credit simply returned Rajesh's money — no coordinator, no held locks, and the money ended up consistent again. The only observable difference was a brief window where the funds were in flight, which is eventual consistency and entirely acceptable.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: two-phase commit buys perfect cross-resource atomicity by making every participant hold locks until a single coordinator decides, which means a coordinator crash after the votes leaves everyone blocked, so for cross-service operations I prefer a Saga of local commits with compensating actions and accept eventual consistency, keeping 2PC only for the rare case of a few XA-capable resources under one operator where atomicity is non-negotiable.

---

keyPoints: Saga: sequence of local transactions + compensating actions
Choreography: events trigger next step — decoupled
Orchestration: central coordinator manages the flow
Outbox pattern: reliable event publishing with DB transaction
